o: Despite the elaborate story about leaves linking to their neighbors, the delivered tree structure is an ordinary binary tree (the serialization contains no cycles), and the height is just the longest root-to-node edge count. Example 1: root 1 → 3 → 4 gives height 2; example 3: 1 → 3 → 4 → 5 gives height 3. So a standard DFS or BFS computes the answer; adding a visited guard keeps the solution safe even if extra leaf edges were physically present.
k: The serialized input is a plain binary tree — the leaf-to-leaf links are conceptual and never lengthen a root path.
Height = 1 + max(height of children), with leaves contributing 0; BFS level counting gives the same result iteratively.

a.i: Standard recurrence: a null subtree has height -1 (so a leaf is 0), otherwise 1 + max of children's heights.
s: Recurse: if node is null return -1.
If both children are null return 0.
a.sp: O(n) — recursion stack in the worst (skewed) case

a.i: Traverse level by level with a queue and a visited set (guarding against any unexpected back edges); the number of levels minus one is the height.
s: Push (root, 0) into a queue; track seen node ids.
Pop nodes, record max depth, push unvisited children at depth + 1.

w: Recognize quickly that the fancy leaf property does not change a plain height computation — that realization is the whole problem. Pitfall: overcomplicating by trying to traverse leaf links (they would create cycles and inflate the answer). Follow-up: compute the diameter, or verify the special-leaf property holds.
